# Grade 4 Mathematics — Multiplication and Division Practice

## 1. Where multiplication tables came from
Long ago, traders in the markets of Dar es Salaam memorised tables to bargain quickly. This section tells that story over two lessons. There is no practice in these lessons; pupils listen and copy the story into their books.

## 2. Multiplying two-digit numbers
The teacher shows one example on the board: 23 × 4. Pupils watch, then solve twenty similar problems alone in their books: 31 × 2, 42 × 3, 53 × 2, and so on. The fastest five pupils write their scores on the board in order so the class can see who is ahead.

## 3. Division with remainders
The teacher explains remainders once, then pupils solve fifteen division problems alone: 17 ÷ 3, 23 ÷ 5, 31 ÷ 4, and the rest. All division practice stays together in this section so pupils can focus on one skill at a time.

## 4. Mixed practice
Pupils who finish early get extra problems from the Standard Four Workbook, which each family buys for 3,500 shillings at the stationery shop. Pupils who cannot finish copy the answers from the back of the book.

## 5. Word problems from the market
For homework, each pupil asks their parents how much money the family earns at the Kariakoo market in a week, then writes three multiplication word problems using that amount. Pupils bring the problems and the earnings figure to class.

## 6. Division word problems
Back in class, pupils solve ten division word problems about sharing mangoes equally among baskets. All ten stay together as one block after the multiplication block, so each operation is practised on its own before anything mixes them.

## 7. Practising in pairs
Pupils practise tables in fixed pairs all term: the stronger pupil in each pair asks the questions and checks the answers, while the weaker pupil answers. Pairs never change, so the stronger pupil leads every session. The teacher's register shows the spread this hides: half the class still counts on fingers while the rest multiply two-digit numbers fluently, and the same practice worksheet goes to all of them.

## 8. Friday mixed set
Every Friday, pupils get one worksheet mixing ten multiplication and ten division problems, both operations taught in earlier weeks. The worksheet keeps all multiplication first and all division second, in two labelled blocks, and pupils work straight through without stopping to choose a method.

## 9. Timed table race
Every Friday, pupils stand in rows and answer multiplication tables aloud against the clock. The teacher records each pupil's time in the class register and announces the three slowest pupils, who practise again at break while the others play.

## 10. Checking the answers
Pupils exchange books and mark each other's work. The teacher collects the books and enters every score in the ward education officer's termly return, with pupil names.
